grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('Vana')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'Vana' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('vaitamba')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'vaitamba' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Vana vaitamba mahumbwe vachidzidzira mabasa ehunyanzvi hwevakuru.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Traditional Childhood Play ('Mahumbwe') as Practical Life Education
cultural_notes.content: In traditional Shona upbringing, children played 'mahumbwe' after the harvest season—a structured role-playing game where boys and girls built miniature huts, cooked small portions of food gathered from the fields, and practiced the real-life responsibilities and skills of adulthood ('mabasa ehunyanzvi hwevakuru').

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'two women and four men' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vakadzi vaviri' = 'two women' (-viri = 2) and 'nevarume vana' = 'and four men' (-na = 4).

active_exercises.correct_answer: We have four books on the table.

active_exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'mumba' and 'panze'?
options: 'mumba' means at school, while 'panze' means at work
'mumba' means inside the house, while 'panze' means outside
'mumba' means on the roof, while 'panze' means in the kitchen
'mumba' means rural village, while 'panze' means city centre
active_exercises.correct_answer: 'mumba' means inside the house, while 'panze' means outside
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mu-' denotes 'inside' ('mumba' = inside the house), whereas 'panze' means 'outside in the yard'.
